question: When the Lord says 'know me also as the knower of the field in all fields' (BhG 13.2 in the 700-verse numbering; 13.3 in this edition) and calls the highest person in the body the supreme self (13.22 / 13.23), is the knower of the field in each body identical with the Lord, or is the Lord the self of the knowers, distinct from them?

sides.position: The knower of the field in all bodies is the Lord himself; its seeming transmigration and difference belong to it only through ignorance (avidyā) and its adjuncts, and knowing this identity is the knowledge the verse speaks of.

The Lord is the self (ātman) of all the knowers of the field, who are his body and modes; 'me' denotes the Lord as having them for his body, so they are one with him as body with self while remaining distinct individual selves.

question: In what sense is the living being 'an eternal portion of me' (mamaivāṃśo jīvaloke jīvabhūtaḥ sanātanaḥ, BhG 15.7)?

sides.position: A portion only as it were: as the sun's reflection in water or the space enclosed by a pot, the individual appears as a part of the Lord through limiting adjuncts; when these are removed it is not other than him.
A real and eternal part of the Lord, related to him as an attribute or mode to its substance; 'eternal' (sanātana) shows that the part and its distinctness are lasting.
A separated portion (vibhinnāṃśa), eternally distinct from and dependent on the Lord and like him only in part, as distinct from the Lord's own forms (svāṃśa).

notes: Commentators' positions summarised from memory by extractor B (no commentary text available in this run); the verses themselves are cited from the segments. The Dvaita side states the school's general doctrine of the soul as vibhinnāṃśa; Madhva's own comment on 15.7 was not consulted (confidence low for that side).

question: Who or what is the imperishable person (akṣara, kūṭastha) of BhG 15.16, set between the perishable (all beings) and the highest person?

sides.position: The Lord's power of māyā, the seed from which the perishable arises and in which the impressions of the desires and actions of transmigrating beings rest; the highest person is distinct from both the perishable and this imperishable.

The perishable are the bound selves joined to non-conscious matter, called 'all beings'; the imperishable is the released self, free from connection with matter and so unchanging (kūṭastha); the Lord is other than both.
The perishable are all souls, whose bodies perish; the imperishable is Lakṣmī, whose body never perishes; the highest person is Viṣṇu, beyond both.
